newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian lev crisis hits importers hardest.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian lev crisis hits importers hardest.

text.p: The dramatic collapse of Bulgaria's lev currency has dealt a heavy blow to all areas of the economy, but those dependent on imports are particularly hard hit.

Petrol stations are closed, long queues form outside bread shops from early morning, and many retailers say they are simply not re-ordering foreign-made goods because they do not know how much further the lev will fall.
In a shop full of unsold refrigerators and household appliances, owner Sylvia Marinova said she had adopted the old Bulgarian saying -- "Live today as tomorrow things can only get worse".
"In the past people discussed brands and models, now they walk into the shop with calculators in hands, calculating exchange rates like lunatics," she said.
Clothing and shoe seller Georgi Petkov said he was offering a 20 to 25 percent discount to try to clear some of his stock and planned to reduce the range by half.
"At the moment you have to be crazy to be a retailer when even Bulgarian producers are giving you bids in dollars and the average Bulgarian is living on $7-8 a month," he said.
Increased foreign currency supply last week helped the lev recover from its February 7 all-time low of 3,200 to the dollar, to close on Friday at 2,400-2,500 on the interbank foreign exchange market.

But the currency has fallen by some 300 percent against the dollar since the beginning of the year, and the central bank plans to introduce a new 50,000 lev note by June. The 10,000 lev note was only introduced in December.

"We are fighting to survive every day," said Galina Vassileva who runs a book and stationery shop in Sofia. "It is funny but I would prefer not to have a big turnover as a big turnover usually just brings in a lot of useless levs.

"The best thing for a trader now would be to close down for a while and wait until the situation stabilises but we cannot afford to do this as we have regular clients and we do not want to lose them."
Official figures show monthly inflation for January 1 to 25 was 43.8 percent. Experts from the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences forecast it will reach near 100 percent in February.

The Neftochim oil refinery has run up huge losses because official price adjustments cannot keep pace with the fall of the lev. The government raised prices by up to 178 percent last week to encourage suppliers to release fuel from stockpiles.

Bulgaria is also struggling with an acute grain shortage after uncontrolled exports two years ago depleted supplies. A poor harvest last year was attributed to bad weather and a lack of funds for fertilisers.

Interim prime minister Stefan Sofianski said on Friday Bulgaria's current grain supplies would run out in 20 days. He said the government was negotiating deals with the United States, Russia and other sources but would need external funding.

The European Union has already approved humanitarian aid worth 20 million ecus ($23 million) and EU officials meet in Brussels on Monday to discuss further assistance for the Balkan nation of 8.5 million people.

Negotiators from the International Monetary Fund are due in Sofia on Monday to discuss preparations for a currency board, a tough fixed exchange rate regime proposed by the Fund last year to brake the lev's collapse and restore confidence.

The mechanism, expected to be introduced after the elections, strictly matches levs in circulation with central bank reserves, severely restricting government spending and preventing the uncontrolled printing of money. ($ = 0.869 European Currency Unit ECUs)
